metadata.title: Opportunities or risks for civic education in electoral democracies? Evidence from Nigeria

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected original survey data from final-year secondary school students in Lagos State, Nigeria (September–October 2019) using a multi-stage sampling design (purposive selection of LGAs, then random selection of public/private schools, then inviting all final-year students present). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or any specific weight variable name, and it does not describe weighting to restore population representativeness. Analyses are conducted with multilevel models (students at level 1, schools at level 2) and clustered standard errors in the class-membership model, which partially addresses clustering but is not the same as applying survey weights. Because the paper is not using ILSA microdata with official weight variables, the results should be interpreted as descriptive/associational for the sampled Lagos schools rather than nationally representative for Nigeria.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; the dependent variables are intended political participation items and intermediate constructs derived from PCA (e.g., knowledge, democratic norms, engagement, institutional trust). Because the paper is not an ILSA PV-based achievement analysis, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), so missing-data handling is treated as not reported rather than inferred.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of final-year secondary school students in Lagos State, Nigeria, surveyed on one specific day/time in September–October 2019; pilot school data (about 30 students) are excluded. The authors purposively selected 6 urban and 3 rural LGAs to ensure SES variation and included LGAs from each of six educational districts. Within each LGA, two public and two private senior secondary schools were randomly selected from Ministry of Education lists, with replacements when private schools were ineligible/unreachable or not found on arrival; gender variation was ensured by restricting the number of boys-only/girls-only schools per LGA. Students were invited to voluntarily participate; response rates were 73% (private) and 78% (public), with most nonresponse due to absence (e.g., external examinations). The paper does not specify additional item-level missingness rules beyond the reported response/nonresponse.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS the study leveraged Socioeconomic status (SES), Parental political engagement, Youth group membership to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that The study uses an original large-scale pencil-and-paper survey of 3,118 final-year secondary school students (average age 16) in Lagos State, Nigeria, collected in September–October 2019. It examines associations between socioeconomic status (SES), political knowledge, political engagement, democratic norms, and institutional trust, and five intended political participation outcomes measured on four-point scales: voting, party membership, campaigning, contacting politicians, and peaceful protest. The authors estimate multilevel linear regression models (students nested in schools) and then use latent class analysis (LCA) to identify three participation profiles, followed by fractional multinomial logistic regression to relate determinants to class membership. Reported effect sizes are generally very small (partial eta squared < 0.01 in the appendix), and the key pattern is that knowledge and democratic norms are positively related to voting/contacting/protesting but negatively related to party membership and campaigning, while institutional trust is positively related to all participation intentions. The paper does not report any machine-learning model performance metrics, and it does not document a missing-data handling strategy, limiting reproducibility and inference about robustness. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an empirical survey study using multilevel regression and latent class analysis rather than machine-learning prediction/classification. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract (ml_techniques is empty) and no ML target-variable performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE/AUC) are reported. The paper also does not use ILSA cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values, so PV handling is not applicable.
